Story of the Flood (Atraḫasīs) – Standard Babylonian I: “When Gods Were Man”

  • Edition:
  • Translation:
  • Generated by tools/ebl_fetch.py on 2026-10-16 – do not edit by hand; re-run the tool instead.

Per line: N = normalized Akkadian reconstruction (| metrical foot, || caesura); T = eBL English translation; L = lemmas with eBL dictionary glosses; then notes, parallel lines, and the manuscripts' transliterations (ATF). Bibliography keys like [RN117: 889] are resolved in bibliography.md (RN117 = George 2003).

1

  • N: enūma | ilū | amēlu
  • T: When gods were man,
  • L: enūma ← inūma I “when Bab.”; ilū ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; amēlu ← awīlu I “man human being (also coll.)”
  • Note: See the discussion of the line in OB I.
SipNB1 o 1. e-nu-ma i-lu a-me#-lu

2

  • N: ilū | nīra || ibnû | tupšikka
  • T: The gods made the yoke, the carrying basket.
  • L: ilū ← ilu I “pl. ilū, ilānu god, deity a or the god, also du.”; nīra ← nīru I “yoke, crossbeam”; ibnû ← banû IV “to create”; tupšikka ← tupšikku I “pl. f. brick-carrying frame”
  • Note: See [RN118: 184]: “The second line of the opening couplet departs significantly from the OB version, which has ublū dulla izbilū šupšikka (I 2). It is easy to see how ub-lu and iz-bi-lu could be corrupted into i-lu and ib-nu-u₂ by a careless editor, but the substitution of dulla by ni-ra cannot be accounted for in the same way. As already translated, there are two ways of taking ni-ra: either it is nīra, i.e., the first object of ibnû (the sandwiching of a verb between two accusatives is also found in SB II 90), or it is nēr, the traditional number of the throng of junior gods. Our preference is marginally for the former, following SB I 41a, where the mutinous gods vow to break the yokes with which they carry their baskets of soil (tupšikku). However that may be, the remodelling of the couplet shows that, by this scribe at least, the first line was understood as a complete clause. The fact that the Assyrian recension nevertheless gives the incipit as enūma ilū kī amīlī, “when the gods like men” ([RN2709: 533–4]), shows that the scribes of the first millennium were almost as divided as modern scholars by the syntax and meaning of the OB inūma ilū awēlum (see above, fn. 1).”
SipNB1 o 2. i-lu ni-ra ib-nu-u₂ tu-up-ši-ik-ku#

SipNB1 o 3. tu-up-ši-ik i-lu ra-bi-i-ma
